attempts.hypothesis: The world is partially observable with biased sensors and imperfect motors, so I build an online occupancy map from the five rays, plan with Dijkstra to the next checkpoint, and add reactive avoidance plus adaptive compass/motor-bias correction.

The world has biased sensors and imperfect motors where online mapping plus reactive avoidance works; I'm replacing Dijkstra with fast 8-connected BFS and adding line-of-sight path smoothing to eliminate the planning timeout that killed attempt 5.

The world has biased sensors and imperfect motors where online occupancy mapping with BFS planning and reactive avoidance works; I'm tightening target approach zones (slow down later at 1.8m/0.9m instead of 2.5m/1.2m), reducing heading-error speed penalty, lengthening look-ahead for smoother high-sp

I believe the world rewards speed through turns and efficient target approach while maintaining safety margins; I'm basing on attempt 6 (best score) and adding slightly more aggressive turning gain, reduced heading-error speed penalty, and tighter target approach zones.
I believe the rover can navigate by steering toward each target while using the five range sensors to slow down and turn toward clearer space around obstacles.
The first controller made abrupt, oscillating turns near obstacles, so I’m adding damped target steering, clearance-based sidesteps, earlier slowing, and a recovery turn if progress stalls.

The rover reached the first checkpoint but crashed after abrupt steering near obstacles; I’m smoothing and limiting turns, slowing earlier, and briefly committing to the clearer side when an obstacle is ahead.
The target steering and persistent sidestep worked on the practice route, so I’m keeping them while adding cautious speed limits near arena edges and braking when the front corridor is very short.

I believe momentum near tight obstacles and arena walls is the main crash risk on unseen courses, so I’m keeping the successful sidestep policy while pulling inward earlier and braking based on speed and clearance.

I believe committing to a clear side is effective, but unseen tight passages need earlier speed-aware avoidance and slower high-angle turns, so I’m strengthening those responses while keeping the proven recovery behavior.
I believe the extra slowdown from far-side rays cost time beside harmless rocks, so I’m relaxing that slowdown while keeping speed-aware avoidance, wall margins, and recovery behavior.
Clear readings appear to leave speed on the table, so I’m raising open-path cruise while keeping the sidestep behavior and braking earlier when clearance shrinks.
I’ll start with a conservative map-backed reactive rover that calibrates compass drift from GPS motion, plans around discovered obstacles, and slows/steers hard near rocks.

I’m replacing the high-gain, GPS-calibration-heavy controller with a slower low-gain PD rover: conservative compass use, persistent inflated obstacle memory, A* waypoints, and explicit stop-and-pivot escape near walls/rocks instead of reversing blindly.

I’m switching to a lighter occupancy map with smaller inflation, faster re-planning, stronger emergency reverse-on-close-obstacle behavior, and lower-gain path tracking so the rover can pass gaps without the previous spinning/local-minimum loops.

I’m replacing the unstable high-gain pivot/recovery logic with a damped pure-pursuit controller over a conservative inflated occupancy map, adding a short, bounded emergency maneuver only when a front ray is critically close.

The rover’s main failure was over-steering and braking too late, so I keep the occupancy/A* planner but replace the controller with a gentler bounded pure-pursuit steering, early all-ray speed limiting, side-centering, short straight reversals, and a brief safe straight start for compass calibration

Attempt 5 succeeded, so I’m preserving its map/A* safety core while adding heading filtering, slightly more open-space speed, smoother speed limits, and extra obstacle-avoidance braking to improve speed without trading away reliability.

I’m reverting the aggressive heading-filter and speed changes from attempt 6, keeping the proven map/A* core, and adding earlier clearance-based braking plus a small away-steer during emergency braking to avoid side impacts before inertia closes the gap.

I’m keeping the successful map/A*/conservative-reactive rover from attempt 7, but slightly relaxing the overly cautious clearance limits, braking, and target approach while still slowing heavily in narrow gaps so unseen layouts are less likely to time out.

I assume a noisy compass with a constant offset that GPS course can correct, short-range rays that need a wide berth, and motors with a small-command deadband, so this controller steers toward each target, repels from rays, and reverses when stuck.

The attempt-1 rover jittered in place because its high-gain, bang-bang steering fought a ray-repulsion term, so I'm adding a ray-built occupancy map with A* planning, lower-gain heading control, GPS-course compass correction, and stuck recovery.

Attempt 2 mostly spun in place: its high-gain bang-bang turns flipped sign every tick and its stuck detector never fired, so I'm keeping the occupancy map and A* but adding gentler heading control, committed back-off and pivot manoeuvres, and a stuck trigger based on sustained forward commands.

Attempt 3's trace shows compass noise of roughly ±20° and a motor deadband, so I'm low-pass filtering heading, slew-limiting commands, lowering the steering gain, and adding a no-progress backup on top of the A* planner.

The logs show turning is very fast (about 90°/s at ±0.35 wheel commands) while my old gains and forced minimum commands made the heading loop oscillate, so this attempt uses physically scaled, low-gain heading control with a lighter repulsion term and a committed stuck escape.

Attempt 6's wall repulsion had its sign reversed, so the rover steered toward nearby walls; this attempt fixes that, uses a 2.5 m pure-pursuit lookahead for smoother steering, and replaces the chaotic pivot logic with simple proportional steering and a single stuck-escape.

The traces show heading oscillating after commands with about 0.5 s of actuator lag, so this attempt uses gentler proportional steering, lower speed, and no forced minimum commands, keeping the map and A* planner while removing the pivot-and-repulse thrashing.
